newsitem.title: USA: Disclosure rules on derivatives due soon from SEC.
newsitem.headline: Disclosure rules on derivatives due soon from SEC.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission plans to release final rules by around the end of the year governing the disclosure of derivatives activity by public U.S. companies, a commission official said on Friday.
"The commission intends to release something final in the next month or within a few months," SEC chief accountant Michael Sutton told Reuters.

Because the rules will not be out until around year-end, the SEC may allow companies to omit portions of the required disclosures from their 1996 annual reports, most likely those including quantitative measures, Sutton said.

"How the rules will apply to 1996 reporting is something that will be dealt with in the final release," Sutton said after a speech at an American Institute of Certified Public Accountants conference here. "People are concerned about having enough time, especially for the quantitative disclosure. It's possible some (required information) will not be in 10Ks for 1996, particularly the quantitative. That is something the commission will consider."
Last December the SEC released preliminary rules that would force thousands of companies to clearly acknowledge their use of derivatives to investors.

The SEC proposed three possible disclosure formats: a table of derivatives positions, an analysis of positions' sensitivity to various market moves, and use of complex, quantitative calculations such as "value at risk."
The commission moved after investors were burned by high-profile losses on derivatives at various public companies in 1994, including Gibson Greetings Inc and Procter & Gamble Co.
In his speech, Sutton said that "it would be difficult to predict exactly" how the commission will alter the December proposal in its final rules.
